prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on trapping atoms at a magic wavelength, and its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B012 with Katori and Ye as a single-part prize. Round 1 answered the chair's main question about what separates the lattice clock from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. The comb gave a way to count optical cycles and Wineland's work showed quantum control of a single ion. The magic-wavelength lattice is a third, different idea: it cancels the light shift and removes Doppler and recoil effects while interrogating thousands of atoms in parallel, and that is what moved systematic uncertainty from the 10^-16 range to 10^-18. Lindroth and Kroll make this point well, and Johansson adds that Ye's group made many-body spin-exchange and density effects a controlled part of the clock. The 10^-18 level has been reproduced and compared across JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, which is the calibration and systematics discipline I look for in an instrument result. As for the Chair's question on maturity, I do not think we should wait for the redefinition of the second or a detected variation of constants. The prize should rest on the demonstrated performance, and the citation should say so. I did not change my preferred configuration from round 1. I moved from IceCube first to B012 first in the opening-to-round-1 step, and round 1 strengthened rather than weakened that choice. The supporters of B018, B022, B055 and B032 accept B012 on merit and none gave a scientific objection to it.
statement.case_against: The overlap and novelty objection is not fully answered, only narrowed. Several members, and Mehlig most clearly, see a decisive improvement in an established measurement rather than a new class of phenomena, and a skeptical reader can still call this a third clock prize. The fundamental-physics payoff consists so far of limits, not discoveries. Credit also reaches beyond two names: Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE teams made real contributions, and trapped-ion clocks reached similar accuracy by another route. I accept that B012 draws agreement partly because it offends nobody, and I will not mistake that for proof that it is the deepest physics on the list. My judgment is that for this year it is the best case that is mature, reproduced and attributable.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B018 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a mature theory-plus-experiment case, distinct from the 2016 prize, and says he would accept B012 if topological matter fails to reach agreement.
responses.response: I take B018 seriously and keep it as my first alternative. The science is mature and the Molenkamp experiment is a real confirmation. What keeps me from leading with it is the credit chain: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe, Zhang has died, and the three-dimensional Fu-Kane-Mele strand cannot be fitted into three names. Johansson and Mehlig raise the same problem. I note your statement that you accept B012 on merit and that you ranked it sixth because it is outside your competence. If the committee wants B018 on the table at the vote, someone needs to show how a citation limited to the two-dimensional Z2 state and its HgTe observation stays fair to Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang. I have not seen that argument yet.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B022 and argues that flat bands and correlated insulators do not depend on the pairing mechanism, while conceding that B012 is the consensus choice and would be acceptable.
responses.response: Your reply that prizes have often been given while mechanism questions were open is fair, and flat bands and correlated insulators are well established. The difficulty is the credit, not the physics. Yuan Cao made the decisive 2018 measurements and is outside the trio, and the early confirming groups and moire theorists add to the problem, so the attribution is no cleaner than for B018. On timing, I read your own estimate of five to ten years as an argument to let the field settle. Your question about novelty relative to earlier prizes is the best objection to my choice. I answer it with the magic-wavelength lattice, which is a distinct concept and not just a better number. I would still want B022 to remain on the list for later years.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B055 (Higgs discovery) for its maturity and the lack of an experimental prize, and says B012 is what he could support most readily if individual attribution is judged indefensible.
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs discovery is the weightiest result on the list and that the experimental discovery is unrewarded. My difficulty is the one you describe yourself: your first trio omitted Virdee and later added him, Lindroth and I named different trios, and Della Negra's claim is as strong as the others. For a prize that must withstand public scrutiny, a split nobody can defend is a real scientific-credit problem, not a procedural one. If an expert report could establish an agreed three-person allocation across ATLAS and CMS I would reopen it. Until then I read your fallback to B012 as the right fallback, and I welcome it.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B032 (aberration-corrected electron optics) as an original instrument invention, acknowledges that Knut Urban is omitted, and names B012 as the most acceptable fallback.
responses.response: As an instrument builder I respect the case. Aberration correction is a real invention that changed what can be seen, and it is reproduced and commercial. I share the concerns that Johansson and Mehlig raise on two points. First, whether it counts as a discovery in physics, as opposed to a tool whose main impact is in materials science and other fields. Second, the exclusion of Knut Urban and the unverified TEM and STEM priority split between Haider, Rose and Krivanek. Your own statement that only one member ranks it high and that your field may bias you makes the weak support understandable. I appreciate that you name B012 as the fallback.

responses.point: Kroll asks that the citation name the lattice-clock architecture and the 10^-18 regime, and reports a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder as a possible adjacency to Ye's lineage.
responses.response: I agree with the citation wording and have changed my own citation accordingly. It now names the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and 10^-18 fractional uncertainty explicitly and drops the fundamental-physics clause I had in round 1, since the payoff is prospective. I also accept your reasoning on your Boulder year: a year in the laboratory of an earlier laureate, with no collaboration with Katori or Ye, is a matter of expertise and not a recusal issue. I would only ask that it stays in the record.

uncertainties: Whether external experts on the clock community support Katori and Ye as the two names, given Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Bloom and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups. I rely on colleagues and expert reports for this.
Whether the committee sees the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. The citation wording is meant to settle this, but members may weigh it differently.
Whether the redefinition of the second and any fundamental-physics result will arrive soon enough to change the balance, in case the committee prefers to wait.
Whether IceCube (B013) will obtain enough confirmed point sources in the next few cycles to become mature, and how to credit earlier DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA work.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I work in astroparticle physics and in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, so I am close to the field of B013 (IceCube) and, more loosely, to B027. B013 is only an alternative in my configuration and I have no known personal tie to its credited names. I have no known tie to Katori, Ye or the other credited names on B012, and I see no recusal need. I note the flags by Johansson (possible recusal for B064), Olsson (field closeness to B032) and Kroll (Boulder year), and none of them affects the configuration I propose.
